title: A comparative study on the performance of cermet and coated carbide inserts in turning of a high-carbon high-silicon cast steel
abstract: Abstract Over the past decades, bainitic steels have gained attention for combining high strength and ductility, although these properties often impair machinability. This study investigated the influence of turning parameters on the machining of high-carbon high-silicon cast steel (HC-HSi) in the homogenized condition prior to bainitic transformation. TiN-coated cermet inserts and multilayer TiN/Al₂O₃/TiCN-coated carbide inserts were compared in terms of cutting-force components, surface roughness, chip temperature, and tool wear. Metallographic analysis revealed a fully pearlitic microstructure with refined interlamellar spacing, which may be associated with the alloy composition. Under less severe cutting conditions, the cermet tool produced lower cutting-force components; however, at higher feed rates and cutting speeds, the coated carbide tool exhibited superior performance. Feed rate was the dominant factor affecting surface roughness, whereas differences between tool materials were not statistically significant at the lowest feed rate. Higher chip temperatures for the cermet tool were attributed to its lower thermal conductivity. The coated carbide tool exhibited approximately 43% lower flank wear, probably owing to its multilayer coating and the formation of protective oxide layers. These findings characterize the machinability of HC-HSi cast steel and support the selection of cutting tools and parameters for achieving lower cutting forces, surface roughness, chip temperature, and tool wear.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In recent decades, the development of advanced steels has been driven by the increasing demand for materials that combine high strength, toughness, and cost-effective manufacturing routes. Among these materials, high-carbon high-silicon (HC–HSi) steels have attracted significant attention for their ability to develop carbide-free bainitic microstructures after appropriate heat treatments, leading to exceptional combinations of mechanical properties [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. The addition of silicon plays a crucial role in suppressing cementite precipitation during bainitic transformation by reducing its thermodynamic stability, thereby promoting carbon enrichment of the retained austenite and enhancing toughness and strength [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ].

Carbide-free bainitic steels typically consist of a mixture of bainitic ferrite and carbon-enriched retained austenite, in which the refined microstructural scale contributes to high tensile strength, hardness, and fatigue resistance [ 6 ,  7 ,  8 – 9 ]. However, achieving such microstructures requires strict control of chemical composition, thermal history, and transformation kinetics, particularly to avoid the formation of undesirable phases such as martensite or coarse pearlite, which may deteriorate mechanical performance [ 6 ]. Consequently, alloying strategies involving elements such as silicon, chromium, manganese, molybdenum, and nickel have been widely adopted to improve austemperability and microstructural refinement [ 1 ,  6 ].

The development of carbide-free bainitic steels has been mainly focused on steels previously homogenized and hot rolled, i.e. thermomechanically processed to minimize solute segregation and refine the solidification microstructure [ 2 ]. Only a limited number of studies have focused on cast steels [ 1 ]. Nevertheless, many steel parts produced for the automotive, mining or oil industries are typically obtained through the casting process, such as crankshafts, camshafts, pump bodies, suspension components, engine blocks, and transmission cases [ 2 ]. Casting is a manufacturing process widely used to make complex or intricate shapes that would be otherwise difficult or uneconomical to make by other methods [ 10 ].

In the present work, the machinability of the HC–HSi cast steel was evaluated in the homogenized condition, which represents a relevant intermediate processing stage before bainitic heat treatment. At this stage, machining performance plays a decisive role in manufacturing efficiency and tool selection.

The successful mechanical machining processes, in terms of productivity and quality, strongly depend on the tribological behavior of the cutting tool material, including both the substrate and the coating [ 11 ]. In this context, the present study focuses on a comparative analysis of the performance of cermet and coated carbide tools for machining this type of steel.

Ozkan et al. [ 12 ] compared the performance of cermet and coated carbide inserts in turning of 50CrV4 steel. The coated carbide tools generated the highest axial, radial, and cutting forces, whereas the lowest force components were attained with cermet inserts. Additionally, the minimum surface roughness (average roughness R a ) values were obtained with cermet, which can be attributed to a lower built-up-edge (BUE) formation tendency in this cutting tool. The formation of BUE at the cutting edge significantly increases surface roughness.

Touggui et al. [ 13 ] compared the behavior of coated carbide and cermet tools in dry turning of AISI 316L austenitic stainless steel and reported that the coated carbide insert produced better surface quality (R a ) and lower cutting force than the cermet insert, which was attributed to the coating type of carbide insert (PVD, TiAlN-TiN). Conversely, the cermet insert exhibited a 1.25 times higher tool life than the coated carbide insert. This can be attributed to the lower diffusion wear and higher thermal expansion coefficient of the cermet compared to the carbide.

Regarding the quality of the machined surface, Paese et al. [ 14 ] evaluated the surface roughness parameters (R a ) and (maximum profile height R z ) in turning of AISI 1045 steel using CVD and PVD coated carbides inserts, as well as PVD coated cermet inserts. The PVD coated carbide tools produced lower R a  values than the cermet tool. However, for the R z  parameter, the optimized machining conditions associated with the cermet tool resulted in better performance than those obtained with the coated carbide tools. In general, higher values of both R a  and R z  were observed when higher feed rates were combined with a smaller tool nose radius.

Xu et al. [ 15 ] reported that, owing to its lower affinity with the machined workpiece, lower friction coefficient against AISI 4140 steel, and better oxidation resistance, the wear of Ti(C,N)-based cermet was primarily crater wear on the rake face and flank wear caused by abrasive wear. This behavior contributed not only to improved surface quality but also to reduced flank wear and prolonged tool life compared to with the coated carbide tool.

Finally, Reis et al. [ 16 ] reported different results when evaluating the surface roughness root mean square roughness (R q ) obtained after machining AISI 4340 steel with coated carbide and cermet tools. The authors observed that the coated carbide tool provided superior quality for the machined surface, although the roughness increased with the cutting length for both tools. The difference in surface roughness was attributed to less pronounced flank wear and greater coating stability on the cutting edge of the coated carbide tool compared to the cermet.

Therefore, several studies have compared the performance of cermet and coated carbide tools; however, the findings are not consensual. In addition, there is still limited information regarding the machinability of high-carbon high-silicon cast steels prior to bainitic transformation. Therefore, the novelty of this study lies in the investigation of the machinability behavior of HC–HSi cast steel specifically designed for carbide-free bainitic transformation, evaluated in the homogenized condition prior to austempering heat treatment. Unlike previous studies, which have focused predominantly on rolled or forged steels, the present work addresses the machinability of HC–HSi cast steel and provides a comprehensive comparison between single-layer TiN-coated cermet and multilayer TiN/Al₂O₃/TiCN-coated carbide tools under dry turning conditions. In addition, the study contributes to the current literature by correlating the machining performance of the homogenized HC–HSi cast steel with the effects of cutting speed and feed rate on cutting forces, surface quality, chip temperature, and tool wear.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The samples used in the turning tests were specially designed and produced by air melting in a 120 kg Inductotherm medium-frequency induction furnace. No mechanical forming was applied. The samples were produced as tubular specimens with a length of 300 mm, an outer diameter of 77 mm, and a wall thickness of 22 mm to ensure material homogeneity across the cross-section. The alloy was designed with high-carbon, high-silicon, and substitutional solutes to promote bainitic transformation. CaSi was added for deoxidation, and Cerium (Ce) for grain refinement. The chemical composition of the as-cast steel was determined using a SpectroMaxx optical emission spectrometer from ARLW, model 3460.

After demolding, the homogenization heat treatment was carried out at 1100 ºC for 24 h to minimize segregation and promote microstructural uniformity. The furnace used for heat treatment was of the crucible type, manufactured by Oriental Engineering®, model P 50–120. The specimens were kept covered and protected by graphite throughout the heat treatment to prevent decarburization, followed by furnace cooling to room temperature. This slow cooling rate promoted the formation of a pearlitic microstructure and prevented martensitic transformation [ 9 ].

In addition, an electronic universal EMIC DL 10,000 testing machine was used to conduct the tensile tests and to investigate the ultimate tensile strength (UTS), yield strength (YS), and total elongation (TEL). The six cylindrical specimens were prepared with a nominal diameter of 6.25 mm and a gauge length of 32 mm according to ASTM A370-2016 [ 20 ]. The fracture surfaces of tensile specimens were analyzed by SEM images after mechanical tests to identify and confirm the fracture mechanism of the HC-HSi cast steel.

Vickers microhardness tests were performed using a Future Tech F111 tester with a load of 0.300 kgf and an indentation time of 15 s as recommended by ASTM E 92–82 [ 21 ]. Hardness measurements were performed considering the minimum recommended spacing of three times the Vickers indentation diagonal length [ 21 ], both from the specimen edge and between adjacent indentation. The aim was to evaluate the microhardness distribution across the specimen cross section. A total of 115 measurements were performed, with a spacing of 150 µm between adjacent indentations.

Longitudinal turning tests were performed using coated cermet and coated carbide cutting inserts of CNMG120408 geometry with chip breakers, both of ISO P20 grade. The cermet and carbide inserts were coated by physical vapor deposition (PVD) and chemical vapor deposition (CVD) techniques, respectively.The inserts were characterized for their substrate and coating structures, as well as the coating thickness, using a Jeol JSM-IT300 SEM coupled with an energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS).

The chemical composition of the cermet substrate was 42.9 wt% titanium, 11.8 wt% carbon, 5.1 wt% nitrogen, 6.7 wt% cobalt, 6.4 wt% nickel and 27.1 wt% mixed carbides. The cermet insert was coated with a single TiN layer with a thickness of 2.85 ± 0.25 µm. The chemical composition of the cemented carbide substrate was 73.1 wt% tungsten carbide, 7.0 wt% cobalt and 19.9 wt% mixed carbides. The multilayer TiN/Al 2 O 3 /TiCN coating had a total thickness of 10.51 ± 0.30 µm (1.50 ± 0.10 µm TiN top-layer, 2.06 ± 0.10 µm intermediate-layer, and 6.95 ± 0.10 µm TiCN base-layer). The PCLNR2020K-12 tool holder was used, resulting in the following effective geometry: point angle = 80º, back rake angle = 9°, clearance angle = 5°, approach angle = 95° and nose radius = 0.8 mm.

Dry turning experiments were performed on a CNC lathe 5.5 kW and a maximum rotational speed of 3,500 rpm. Figure  2  shows the experimental turning setup. A full factorial experimental design was employed, and each turning condition was replicated once, thus resulting in 48 runs. Fig. 2 Turning force measurement system experimental setup

The cutting operation was carried out at different cutting speeds (v c ) of 150, 200, 250 and 300 m min −1 , feed rates (f) of 0.15, 0.25 and 0.35 mm rev −1 , and a constant depth of cut (a p ) of 1.5 mm. The cutting speed and feed rate ranges were selected based on the recommendations provided by the tool manufacturer. A new insert was used for each test to avoid the influence of tool wear. Each experimental condition was evaluated through an experimental run and its corresponding replicate under identical setup and controlled conditions to minimize external variability and ensure consistency of the obtained results. Although the adopted procedure provided consistent results, additional independent replicates would enhance the statistical robustness of the analyses.

Measurements of cutting force (F c ), feed force (F f ) and passive force (F p ) were carried out using a Kistler piezoelectric dynamometer type 9272, amplifier 5073 Kistler, and USB-6366 acquisition boards. The SignalExpress 2015 software by National Instrument was used to process the data.

The surface roughness parameters R a  and R z  of the machined surfaces were measured during the turning using a portable Taylor Hobson Precision® Surtronic 25 roughness tester. Cutoff lengths of 0.8 and 2.5 mm and evaluation lengths of 4 and 12.5 mm were used for R a  and R z  measurements, respectively. Profile roughness measurement was made on the workpiece over a 15 mm length. The measurement of the workpiece surfaces was repeated four times along axial lines positioned at 90º apart around the cylindrical surface. Average R a  and R z  values were obtained by taking the arithmetic averages of these measurements.

For temperature measurements, a Raytek MM2ML infrared pyrometer was used. The device has an operating range of 300 °C to 1100 °C, with a response time of 2 ms, a measurement accuracy of ± (0.3% of the reading + 2 °C), a repeatability of ± (0.1% of the reading + 1 °C), and a temperature resolution of 0.1 °C. According to the manufacturer, the recommended focal distance between the pyrometer and the target surface is 300 mm. Accurate chip temperature measurement required knowledge of the cast steel emissivity and appropriate adjustment of this parameter in the software. Temperature data acquisition was performed using Multidrop Rev. 5.3.1 software developed by DataTemp®.

The emissivity value adopted in the infrared temperature measurements was determined through a prior calibration procedure. A cast steel specimen was heated using an electrical heating system controlled by a variable voltage supply. The specimen temperature was monitored simultaneously by a K-type thermocouple inserted into the specimen and connected to a KRAD01 Kript portable ammeter/temperature indicator, and by the Raytek MM2ML infrared pyrometer. The emissivity value in the Multidrop software was progressively adjusted until the temperature measured by the pyrometer matched that indicated by the thermocouple under steady-state conditions. The emissivity value obtained from this calibration procedure was 0.135 and was subsequently used in all chip temperature measurements. Photographs of the emissivity calibration setup are provided in the Supplementary Material.

The pyrometer setup used for chip temperature measurements is depicted in Fig.  3 , which illustrates the circumferential direction adopted for temperature acquisition. The cutting condition of v c  of 300 m min −1  was excluded from the chip temperature analysis due to unstable infrared signal behavior under high chip velocity conditions, which compromised measurement repeatability and reliability. Therefore, the data were not considered suitable for quantitative comparison. Fig. 3 Set up of pyrometer for chip temperature measurement and the focal point region

For wear assessment, the tool life criterion was defined as the occurrence of either of the following conditions: (i) the average flank wear width (VB B ) reached 0.30 mm, in accordance with ISO 3685, considering uniform wear land development in zone B, or (ii) the cutting tools were not able to further cut properly.

A preliminary test was conducted to monitor the wear of cermet and coated carbide tools. Initially, cutting parameters were set to v c  of 200 m min −1 ,  f  of 0.15 mm rev −1 , a p  of 1.5 mm and cutting length of 135 mm, with coated carbide tool being tested first. With this configuration, only 4 passes were possible before the tool met condition (ii). Subsequently, parameters for wear assessment were adjusted to v c  of 150 m min −1 ,  f  of 0.15 mm rev −1 , a p  of 1.0 mm and cutting length of 135 mm.

During wear evaluation, VB B  was monitored through images obtained with a microscope at magnification of 25-500x, with monitoring conducted after every two passes of the cutting tool. Four VB B  measurements were obtained using AxioVision SE64 software: two on the flank face of the tool used in the test and two in the same region of the corresponding replicate tool. The arithmetic mean and standard deviation were subsequently calculated.

Microscope and SEM images were considered direct methods for wear assessment, whereas EDS analyses were used to support the identification of wear mechanisms. As an indirect wear monitoring method, machining force values for each pass were utilized with the evaluated cutting tools. The final VB B  was measured using SEM images after wear test along with EDS analysis. Before SEM imaging, both tools were immersed in a solution of PA Ethanol for ultrasonic cleaning. The Limp Sonic ultrasonic cleaner, model LS-1.3 D-3/x. 1800, was used for 2 h.

The surface roughness of the workpiece was evaluated through 2D profile and 3D topography analyses after the final pass of the cermet and coated carbide tools. Measurements were performed using a Hommelwerk T8000 profilometer, and the images and parameters were processed with Hommelmap Expert 6.2 software. Twenty-five measurements were taken for each tool. The roughness parameters R a , R z , R t , Skewness (Ssk) and kurtosis (Sku) were selected to investigate the correlation between the surface topography of the HC-HSi cast steel and the machining process using cermet and coated carbide tools.

sections.heading: Chemical, microstructural and mechanical characterization
paragraphs: The main alloying elements in this steel (Table  1 ), including carbon, chromium, molybdenum, manganese, nickel and silicon, contribute significantly to the development and morphology of the pearlitic microstructure (Fig.  4 ). In particular, carbon, manganese, chromium and silicon influence the refinement and homogeneity of ferrite and cementite lamellae, as well as the interlamellar spacing, mainly by affecting the transformation kinetics during the eutectoid reaction, as reported by Han, Smith and Edmonds [ 22 ] and Qiao et al. [ 23 ]. Cerium was added to promote grain refinement and improve microstructural uniformity by modifying inclusions and enhancing nucleation sites. This material can be considered a near eutectoid steel, although its carbon content is not exactly 0.80 wt%. Table 1 Chemical composition and mechanical properties of the HC-HSi cast steel used in the turning tests Fe C Si Mn P S Cr Ni Mo Al Ce 94.75 0.75 1.83 0.81 0.03 0.01 0.99 0.52 0.20 0.01 0.004 Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) Yield strength (YS) Elongation Vickers Microhardness 831.98 ± 99.61 MPA 507 ± 22 MPA 2.83 ± 0.66% 295 ± 20 HV Fig. 4 Micrographs of steel with 2% Nital etching:  a ) optical microscope with magnification of 400x;  b ) SEM with magnification of 1000x
The alloy design aimed to obtain a bainitic microstructure after austempering heat treatment.
The eutectoid composition was designed to lower the martensite start temperature (Ms) and thus obtain a more refined bainitic microstructure.

Metallographic analysis of the steel revealed a fully pearlitic microstructure, consisting of alternating lamellae of ferrite (α) and cementite (Fe 3 C), a homogeneous structure, as detailed in Fig.  4 a and b. All analysed microstructures of the steel consisted predominantly of fine pearlite, with some colonies of coarse pearlite. No pro-eutectoid ferrite was observed at the grain boundaries, and a small amount of non-metallic inclusions (black points) was present. The pearlitic microstructure was expected since the chemical composition indicates eutectoid steel. The presence of non-metallic inclusions is characteristic of the casting process [ 2 ]. EDS analyses of the sample confirmed the presence of manganese sulphides, with Mn and S contents of 46.3% and 31.3%, respectively.

In this context, the UTS (831.98 ± 99.61 MPa) and YS (507 ± 22 MPa) obtained for the HC-HSi cast steel may be associated with its fine pearlite interlamellar spacing (0.41 ± 0.08 µm), although a smaller effect was observed on TEL (2.83 ± 0.66%). Similar behavior was reported by Barroso et al. [ 26 ], who observed that a high-carbon (0.77%) and high-silicon (1.75%) cast steel with a fully pearlitic microstructure, after homogenization heat treatment, exhibited UTS values of 949.43 MPa and TEL of 3.26%.

The relatively brittle behavior of the HC-HSi cast steel may be related to the presence of alloying elements that promote the formation of a predominantly pearlitic microstructure and contribute to solid-solution strengthening. These mechanisms increase UTS and YS but reduce ductility due to the higher hardness and lower plastic deformation capability of the matrix (TEL). The SEM images obtained from the fracture surface of a tensile specimen are shown in Fig.  5 a and b, evidencing the brittle behavior of the material, characterized by cleavage facets and river-like patterns (Fig.  5 b). A similar fracture surface was observed in eutectoid steel cooled in the furnace [ 27 ]. No dimples were observed. Fig. 5 SEM fractography analysis of the tensile fracture surface:  a ) general view;  b ) detail of the red dashed region in (a)

The microhardness profile of the HC-HSi cast steel is shown in Fig.  6 . The first measurement was performed at the minimum distance from the surface, in accordance with ASTM E92-82 [ 21 ]. The average hardness obtained was 259 ± 20 HV, with variations ranging from 10 to 30%. Despite these fluctuations, the hardness distribution remained relatively uniform throughout the specimen thickness. Fig. 6 Microhardness profile of HC-HSi cast steel

Naseem et al. [ 28 ] reported a hardness of about 302 HV for high-carbon (0.79%) and high-silicon (1.60%) steel in the annealed, fully pearlitic condition. Similarly, Barroso [ 26 ] observed a hardness of about 294 HV for a high-carbon (0.77%) and high-silicon (1.75%) cast steel after homogenization heat treatment. These values are consistent with those obtained in the present study.

sections.heading: Machinability analyses
paragraphs: Table  2  presents the results of the turning force components, including cutting force (F c ), feed force (F f ) and passive force (F p ). Table  3  reports the values of average roughness (R a ) and maximum profile height (R z ), while Table  4  shows the maximum chip temperature values obtained in the tests.

Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied to determine the influence of the cutting parameters and their interactions, such as cutting speeds (v c ) and feed rates (f), on the output responses, adopting a 95% confidence level. The statistical validity of the ANOVA results was ensured by verifying the underlying assumptions of normality, independence, and homogeneity of variance. Residual normality was assessed using the Anderson–Darling test for all response variables (F c , F f , F p , R a , R z  and chip temperature); with all p-values exceeding the 0.05 significance level, the null hypothesis was not rejected. The independence of residuals was confirmed through residuals-versus-observation order plots, which displayed a random distribution without trends or autocorrelation. Furthermore, homogeneity of variance was validated via residuals-versus-fitted-values plots, indicating a constant spread. Standardized residual analysis further corroborated these findings, with approximately 95% of observations falling within ± 2 standard deviations. These results, supported by the diagnostic plots provided in the Supplementary Material, confirm the adequacy of the ANOVA model and the reliability of the statistical conclusions.

Tables  5 ,  6  and  7  present the results of the ANOVA for the turning force components, roughness parameters and chip temperature of the HC-HSi cast steel obtained using cermet and coated carbide tools. The R 2  values obtained in this study indicate that the adopted statistical model explains between 79 and 99% of the experimental data.  P -values lower than 0.05 are underlined in Tables  5 ,  6 , and  7 , indicating statistically significant effects.

sections.heading: Turning force components
paragraphs: According to Table  3 , the main factors, cutting speed and feed rate, had a statistically significant effect on cutting force, with p-values of 0.000 < α = 0.05.

The cutting tool, however, did not significantly affect cutting force ( p  = 0.096), and no significant interactions involving this factor were observed. In contrast, both the main factors and the second-order interactions (tool × cutting speed and feed rate × tool) significantly affected the feed force. Likewise, all main factors and the second-order interactions (feed rate × cutting speed and tool × feed rate) showed a significant influence on the passive force.

Figure  7  presents the significant factors affecting cutting force. It can be observed that the average cutting force decreased with increasing cutting speed, regardless of feed rate. According to Saini et al. [ 29 ], increasing cutting speed raises the temperature in the cutting zone, promoting workpiece softening and reducing its resistance to plastic deformation, which leads to lower cutting forces. Similar results were reported by Das et al. [ 30 ]. Fig. 7 Effect of feed rate and cutting speed in relation to cutting force

Additionally, the positive rake angle (9°) reduces the tool-chip contact length, decreasing friction and shear stresses and consequently lowering the cutting force, as discussed by Saini et al. [ 29 ] and Shaw [ 31 ]. As a result, both shear stress and frictional forces at the interface were reduced, facilitating chip formation and consequently lowering the cutting force.

Regarding the feed rate, it was the most influential factor in increasing the turning force components, as expected. The feed rate contributed 96.62% of the total variation in cutting force (Table  3 ). When the feed rate was increased from 0.15 to 0.25 mm rev⁻ 1 , the average cutting force increased by approximately 50% (from 683 ± 36 N to 1029 ± 43 N). A further increase from 0.25 to 0.35 mm rev⁻ 1  led to an additional rise of about 40% (from 1029 ± 43 N to 1442 ± 65 N). This behavior can be attributed to the increase in the tool–chip contact area on the rake face and the enlargement of the chip shear area, which increase the resistant to plastic deformation and requires higher mechanical effort for chip removal [ 13 ]. Similar results were reported by Touggui et al. [ 13 ], who also observed an increase in cutting force at higher feed rates when machining with coated cermet and coated carbide inserts.

Figure  8 a and b show the significant interactions affecting the feed force. No statistically significant differences were observed between cermet and coated carbide tools across the evaluated cutting speeds. A two-sample t-test performed at a 5% significance level yielded p-values of 0.792, 0.649, 0.603, and 0.618 for cutting speeds of 150, 200, 250, and 300 m min⁻ 1 , respectively, indicating similar performance for both tools in terms of feed force. The similarity between the tools may be associated with the lower thermal conductivity of cermet [ 32 ], which promotes localized heat accumulation and thermal softening of the workpiece material, resulting in feed forces similar to those obtained with coated carbide tools. For both tools, feed force increased with cutting speed, reaching the highest values at 300 m min⁻ 1 . This behavior may be related to the more severe cutting conditions at higher speeds, which can increase friction at the tool-workpiece interface and consequently raise feed force values, as reported by Chinchanikar and Choudhury [ 33 ]. Fig. 8 Feed force interaction plots:  a ) tool and cutting speed;  b ) tool and feed rate

With respect to the influence of feed rate (Fig.  8 b), this factor accounted for a percentage contribution of 88.31% (Table  3 ). Regarding the cutting tools, cermet and coated carbide showed only slight differences at the evaluated feed rates. A two-sample t-test yielded p-values of 0.587, 0.269, and 0.032 for feed rates of 0.15, 0.25, and 0.35 mm rev⁻1, respectively. Therefore, no statistically significant differences were found between the tools at the two lowest feed rates. These results indicate that no statistically significant differences in mean feed force were found between the tools at the lowest and intermediate feed rates. However, at the highest feed rate, a statistically significant difference was observed, with the cermet tool producing a feed force approximately 9.7% higher than the coated carbide tool.

Additionally, the higher feed force values can be attributed to the depth of cut (1.5 mm), which exceeded the tool nose radius (0.8 mm), causing part of the straight cutting edge to engage in the cut and increasing the load on the tool, as reported by Chinchanikar and Choudhury [ 33 ].

Figure  9 a and b show the significant interactions affecting the passive force. Only slight differences were observed for cutting speeds between 150 and 250 m min⁻ 1 , regardless of feed rate. However, the highest passive force values were consistently obtained at 300 m min⁻ 1  for all evaluated feed rates, indicating that cutting speed had a more pronounced effect under the most severe machining condition investigated. Fig. 9 Passive force interaction plots:  a ) feed rate and cutting speed;  b ) tools and feed rate

Regarding the effect of the feed rate (Fig.  9 b), this factor accounted for a percentage contribution of 69.10% (Table  3 ). As expected, increasing the feed rate resulted in higher average passive force values, with an increase of approximately 48% (from 238 ± 27 N to 351 ± 57 N) when the feed rate was raised from 0.15 to 0.25 mm rev −1 , and about 64% (from 351 ± 57 N to 575 ± 94 N) when it was further increased from 0.25 to 0.35 mm rev −1 .

With respect to the cutting tools, only slight differences were observed in the mean passive force values. A two-sample t-test yielded p-values of 0.741, 0.569, and 0.354 for the evaluated feed rates, indicating no statistically significant differences between cermet and coated carbide tools at a 5% significance level.

Table  8  presents the flank wear (VB) values for the cermet and coated carbide tools obtained from SEM images after the turning tests under conditions (i), (ii), and (iii). Under conditions (i) and (ii), both tools exhibited low VB values, consistent with the similar force components observed for both tool materials. In contrast, under condition (iii), the cermet tool showed greater flank wear, which may explain the higher feed and passive force values obtained under this condition. These results suggest that cermet tools are more susceptible to wear at higher cutting speeds and feed rates, which can influence machining performance and tool life. sections.heading: Roughness
paragraphs: The main factors, cutting tools and feed rate, significantly affected the surface roughness parameters R a  and R z,  with p-values of 0.043, 0.000 and 0.008 < α = 0.05, respectively. The cutting speed did not significantly affect the roughness parameters R a  and R z,  with p-values of 0.403 and 0.235 respectively. Furthermore, no interaction effects were found to be significant. Figure  10 a and b show the behavior of the significant main factors influencing the surface roughness parameters R a  and R z . Fig. 10 Effect of the main factors on surface roughness:  a ) R a  and  b ) R z

Among the evaluated factors, feed rate was the most influential on the surface roughness parameters R a  and R z , with percentage contributions of 89.18% and 90.92%, respectively. This result is consistent with Shaw [ 31 ], who reported that both average roughness and peak-to-valley roughness depend directly and quadratically on the tool feed rate. According to Touggui et al. [ 13 ], increasing feed rate promotes the formation of deeper feed marks on the machined surface, resulting in higher R a  and R z  values. Similar trends have also been reported in previous studies [ 30 ,  34 ].

Regarding the cutting tool, the coated carbide insert provided better surface quality than the cermet tool at feed rates of 0.25 and 0.35 mm rev⁻ 1 , as shown in Fig.  10 a and b. However, at 0.15 mm rev⁻ 1 , the differences were not statistically significant, with p-values of 0.309 and 0.397 for R a  and R z , respectively, indicating similar surface roughness performance for both tools.

At the lowest feed rate (0.15 mm rev⁻ 1 ), the cermet tool exhibited lower mean turning force components (Table  4 ) while producing R a  and R z  values comparable to those obtained with the coated carbide tool. This result is consistent with previous studies reporting an association between lower machining forces and improved surface finish [ 12 ].

sections.heading: Chip temperature
paragraphs: Table  7  presents the ANOVA results for the main effects and factor interactions on chip temperature at a 95% confidence level. Cutting speed and cutting tool were the only statistically significant factors (p < 0.05), whereas no significant second- or third-order interactions were observed. Figure  11  illustrates the main effects influencing chip temperature. Fig. 11 Chip temperature in relation to the main effects v c  and cutting tool

Cutting speed was the most influential factor, contributing 36.06% to chip temperature variation, followed by the cutting tool with 23.35%. Chip temperature increased with cutting speed in the range of 150 to 250 m min⁻ 1 , likely due to the greater heat generation associated with higher cutting energy, in agreement with previous studies [ 30 ,  34 ].

For both coated carbide and cermet tools, chip temperature increased with increasing cutting speed, with consistently higher temperatures observed for the cermet tool at all cutting speed levels. Cutting temperature is strongly influenced by the thermal conductivity of the tool and coating materials, which affects the tribological conditions at the tool-chip interface [ 35 ]. Cermets exhibit lower thermal conductivity (10–15 W·m⁻ 1 ·K⁻ 1 ) compared to cemented carbides (25–80 W·m⁻ 1 ·K⁻ 1 ) [ 36 ], which implies that a greater fraction of the generated heat is carried away by the chip rather than conducted into the tool.

Although only chip temperature was measured in the present study, heat partition theory provides a plausible explanation for the observed results. Grzesik et al. [ 35 ] demonstrated that lower thermal conductivity reduces the fraction of heat transferred into the tool, whereas Hao and Liu [ 37 ] identified thermal conductivity as a critical parameter governing heat partition.

According to Grzesik and Nieslony [ 38 ], lower thermal conductivity reduces the fraction of heat transferred into the tool, while Hao and Liu [ 37 ] demonstrated that thermal conductivity is a key parameter governing heat partition behavior.
Therefore, the higher chip temperatures observed for the cermet tool are consistent with its lower thermal conductivity, which favors a greater transfer of heat to the chip.

sections.heading: Monitoring the evolution of wear
paragraphs: Figure  12  presents the evolution of machining forces as a function of the number of passes for the cermet tool under cutting conditions of v c  150 m·min⁻ 1 ,  f  0.15 mm·rev⁻ 1 , and a p  1.0 mm. A total of 16 passes were performed, corresponding to a cutting length of 2,160 mm. The measured VB B  values for the cermet tool were 0.090 ± 0.001 mm after 2 passes, 0.240 ± 0.010 mm after 10 passes, and 0.295 ± 0.020 mm at the final pass. Fig. 12 Monitoring of machining forces as a function of the number of passes and VB B  wear values for the cermet tool

According to Toubhans et al. [ 39 ], machining forces generally increase as tool wear progresses, and their typical evolution consists of a short run-in period followed by a steady wear region and, finally, the end of the tool’s useful life. In the present study, during the initial passes, a characteristic run-in phase was observed for the cermet tool. The behavior of the cutting forces is consistent with the literature, where the cutting force exhibits the highest values, followed by the feed and passive forces [ 40 ].

However, from the fifth pass onward, the feed and passive forces increased rapidly, surpassing the cutting force. In the final passes, these forces exceeded 600 N (see Fig.  12 ). This behavior can be attributed to the accelerated progression of flank and crater wear starting from the fifth pass, with the VB B  value reaching 0.240 mm by the tenth pass.

According to Dimla [ 41 ], experimental studies have shown that the three components of machining forces respond differently to the various forms of tool wear, with feed and passive forces being more affected than the cutting force. Similarly, Chinchanikar and Choudhury [ 33 ] reported that the increase in feed and passive forces is associated with changes in friction conditions due to tool wear and alterations in the cutting edge geometry.

Figure  13  presents the evolution of machining forces as a function of the number of passes for the coated carbide tool under cutting conditions of v c  150 m·min⁻ 1 ,  f  0.15 mm·rev⁻ 1 , and a p  1.0 mm. A total of 18 passes were performed, corresponding to a cutting length of 2,430 mm. This number of passes was defined to enable a direct comparison of VB B  wear between the coated carbide and cermet tools, since the cermet tool was no longer able to ensure adequate machining after 16 passes. The measured VB B  values for the coated carbide tool were 0.040 ± 0.001 mm after 2 passes, 0.110 ± 0.002 mm after 10 passes, and 0.168 ± 0.004 mm at the final pass. Fig. 13 Monitoring of machining forces as a function of the number of passes and VBB wear values for the coated carbide tool

A brief running-in period was identified during passes 1–3, followed by a stage of controlled wear extending from passes 4–10. Subsequently, a gradual increase in machining forces was noted, consistent with previous reports relating machining forces to tool wear [ 39 ]. As the number of passes increased, the feed and passive forces exhibited a nearly linear rise, whereas the cutting force showed a slight decrease and tended to stabilize at values close to those observed during the initial wear stage.

The evolution of VB B  as a function of the number of cutting passes was analyzed to evaluate tool life performance and is presented in Fig.  14 . The cermet tool reached an average flank wear of 295 μm after 16 passes, a value close to the adopted tool end-of-life criterion of VB = 0.30 mm. In contrast, the coated carbide tool exhibited a significantly lower average flank wear of 168 μm after 18 passes and did not reach the end-of-life criterion within the tested interval. These results indicate a lower wear progression rate and a longer tool life for the coated carbide tool. Fig. 14 Tool wear progression curves as a function of the number of cutting passes

The differences in wear progression may be related to the thermal properties of the tool materials. The cermet tool exhibited higher chip temperatures due to its lower thermal conductivity. The resulting increase in thermal loading at the tool–chip interface likely accelerated wear progression, leading to earlier attainment of the tool end-of-life criterion compared with the coated carbide tool.

sections.heading: Characterization of wear mechanisms
paragraphs: Figure  15 a and b presents SEM images of the rake face together with EDS analyses (spectra 15 and 16) of the cermet tool under the cutting conditions of v c  150 m min⁻ 1 ,  f  0.15 mm rev⁻ 1 , and a p  1.0 mm, providing a more comprehensive assessment of the wear mechanisms involved. The EDS results for spectra 15 and 16 reveal the presence of substrate elements, such as Ti, C, W, Mo, Nb, Ni, and Co, indicating removal of the coating. Furthermore, spectrum 16 shows the presence of workpiece elements, including Si and Fe, suggesting the occurrence of adhesion. Similar findings were reported by Reis et al. [ 16 ], who observed adhesion of workpiece material in the crater region, along with exposure of the cermet tool substrate. Fig. 15 Rake face wear of the cermet tool: ( a ) SEM image with EDS spectra locations; ( b ) detailed view of the crater wear region

Figure  15 b presents the SEM micrograph of the rake surface within the crater wear region, exhibiting a smooth morphology and the absence of grooves, which suggesting a possible contribution of diffusion wear mechanism. The SEM images revealed a deeper crater on the cermet tool. And the absence of the thin TiN coating layer (2.85 ± 0.25 µm) supports the assumption that the removal of the coating favors diffusion wear. The removal of the thin TiN coating layer exposed the cermet substrate directly to the severe thermo-mechanical conditions at the tool-chip interface. Once the coating was lost, the substrate became more susceptible to atomic migration and chemical interaction with the chip, which may have increased the susceptibility of the substrate to crater wear.

Considering that crater formation arises from the continuous sliding of the chip over the rake face, both diffusion and adhesion mechanisms are likely to contribute to the development and progression of crater wear [ 42 ].

It is well established that crater wear results from friction between the chip and the rake face, typically occurring in regions of highest temperature [ 43 ]. As demonstrated in Sect.  3.2.3 , higher chip temperatures were observed for the cermet tool, which can be attributed to its lower thermal conductivity and the greater heat transfer to the chip. This increase in temperature consequently intensifies the crater wear.

Another aspect related to the influence of temperature on crater wear is evidenced by the EDS analysis. Spectrum 16 shows a higher oxygen content compared to spectrum 15 and corresponds to the region where crater wear is more pronounced, suggesting the occurrence of oxidative wear. According to Yang et al. [ 44 ], the presence of oxygen is associated with the formation of metallic oxides such as TiO₂ (titanium dioxide), WO₃ (tungsten trioxide), and MoO₃ (molybdenum trioxide), generated by oxidation reactions at elevated temperatures during the turning process.

Corrêa, Schroeter, and Machado [ 45 ] reported that oxidative wear occurs when these oxide layers are subsequently removed, as they are formed through reactions between the tool material and atmospheric oxygen at high temperatures. Furthermore, Trent and Wright [ 46 ] note that oxidative wear becomes more severe once the oxide films are disrupted. The rupture of adhesive junctions between the oxides and the tool surface may also lead to the removal of material grains, characterizing the attrition wear mechanism. The higher oxygen concentration detected in spectrum 16, together with the elevated chip temperatures measured for the cermet tool, suggests that oxidation was thermally activated in the crater region. Repeated formation and removal of oxide layers may have accelerated material loss and contributed to the more severe crater wear observed for this tool.

Figure  16  presents the SEM images and EDS analyses of the clearance face of the cermet tool. EDS spectrum 28 reveals the presence of substrate elements, such as Ti, C, W, Mo, Nb, and Ni, indicating partial removal of the coating. The SEM image in Fig.  16  shows distinct grooves, which are characteristic of an abrasive wear mechanism, likely caused by hard carbide particles and intensified by the high temperatures generated during machining, as reported by Chen, Xu, and Xiao [ 42 ]. Spectrum 29, in turn, reveals elements characteristic of HC-HSi steel, such as Fe, O, Si, Cr, Mn, and Mo, indicating the occurrence of adhesion wear mechanisms. Fig. 16 SEM and EDS images of the clearance face of the cermet tool

In addition, partial wear of the cutting edge was observed, indicating that crater wear extended toward the clearance face of the cermet tool. Similar findings were reported by Sarjana et al. [ 47 ], who identified chipping that deteriorated both the rake face and the interface between the flank region and the main cutting edge. According to these authors, chipping or crater wear is initiated by coating degradation at the chip-tool interface during chip formation, followed by progressive substrate wear. As the cutting process continues, this wear can lead to edge fracture or chipping. Therefore, for the cermet tool, adhesion, abrasion, diffusion, attrition and chipping are suggested as the main mechanisms governing its wear behavior.

Figure  17  presents the SEM images and EDS analyses of the rake surface of the coated carbide tool. The EDS results corresponding to spectra 18 and 20 indicate the presence of Ti and N elements, suggesting that the TiN coating was not completely removed. This observation indicates that tool wear was not severe, as supported by relatively low VB B  value of 0.168 ± 0.004 mm and the absence of substrate exposure on the tool surface. Fig. 17 SEM and EDS images of the rake surface of the coated carbide tool

Another noteworthy observation is that the SEM image of the rake surface in the crater wear region exhibits a smooth morphology and the absence of grooves, which is indicative of diffusion wear mechanism. The presence of Fe and O elements suggested the formation of iron oxides on the tool surface, as Fe is the main element of HC-HSi steel. The presence of O promotes the formation of a thin oxide layer (typically 1.0 to 10.0 nm thick) on metallic surface [ 48 ]. These oxide layers may act as protective barrier, preventing direct metal-to- metal contact and inhibiting the formation of adhesive bonds, or they may fracture and lead to abrasion wear, depending on their hardness [ 49 ]. In this context, it is suggested that the formation of oxide layers contributed to minimizing crater wear on the coated carbide tool. Additionally, the coating thickness of the coated carbide tool, approximately 10.51 ± 0.30 µm, may have further contributed to limiting the depth and severity of crater wear.

Figure  18  presents the SEM images and EDS analyses of the clearance surface of the coated carbide tool. The EDS results corresponding to spectrum 30 indicate the presence of TiN coating elements .  The absence of elements such as W, Co, Zr, and Nb suggests that the tool substrate was not exposed. Spectrum 31, in turn, indicates the occurrence of material adhesion, as evidenced by the presence of Fe, C, O, Si, Mn, and Cr ,  which are characteristic elements of HC-HSi steel . Fig. 18 SEM and EDS images of the clearance surface of the coated carbide tool

In the study by Diniz, Micaroni, and Hassui [ 50 ], material adhesion was also observed in the flank region of the coated carbide tool. The presence of Fe and O elements further indicates the formation of iron oxides. Therefore, adhesion, oxide layer formation, and abrasion are suggested as the main mechanisms governing the wear behavior of the coated carbide tool.

Therefore, based on the wear analysis conducted under cutting conditions of v c  150 m min⁻ 1 ,  f  0.15 mm rev⁻ 1 , and a p  1.0 mm, the coated carbide tool demonstrated to be more suitable for machining HC-HSi steel. The wear progression curves showed that the cermet tool reached 295 μm after 16 passes, whereas the coated carbide tool reached a final VBB value of 168 μm after 18 passes, exhibited approximately 43% lower flank wear. This superior performance can be attributed to the combined effects of the multilayer coating and the higher thermal conductivity of the coated carbide substrate, which promoted more efficient heat dissipation away from the tool–chip interface and resulted in lower chip temperatures. In addition, the formation of oxide layers identified by EDS contributed to protecting the tool surface and delaying substrate exposure. Consequently, the lower thermal load experienced by the coated carbide tool reduced the severity of diffusion and oxidation wear mechanisms, leading to less pronounced flank and crater wear and ultimately extending tool life compared with the cermet tool under the investigated cutting conditions.

sections.heading: Machined surface roughness
paragraphs: Figure  19  presents the 2D profile analyses and 3D surface topographies obtained in the final pass for both the cermet and coated carbide tools. The cermet tool exhibited surface roughness values of R a  = 0.95 ± 0.02 µm, R z  = 4.40 ± 0.16 µm, and R t  = 4.77 ± 0.18 µm, whereas the coated carbide tool produced lower values of R a  = 0.66 ± 0.02 µm, R z  = 3.67 ± 0.21 µm, and R t  = 4.14 ± 0.41 µm. These results indicate a superior surface finish for the coated carbide tool, consistent with its reduced flank and crater wear. Fig. 19 2D profile and 3D Topography of tools after wear test:  a ) cermet;  b ) coated carbide

The VB B  of 0.295 mm and more pronounced crater wear observed in the cermet tool promoted the formation of a rounded and unstable cutting edge, leading to deeper valleys in the machined surface, as reflected by the higher R z  and R t  values, and consequently an increased R a . In contrast, the coated carbide tool, which exhibited lower flank wear (VB B  = 0.168 mm) and less severe crater wear, maintained more stable cutting conditions, resulting in surface profiles with lower amplitude (R z  and R t ) and reduced R a .

Beyond the amplitude parameters R a , R z , and R t , the statistical descriptors of the surface profile provide additional insights into the interaction between tool wear and the resulting topography. The negative skewness values obtained for both tools (Ssk = –0.66 ± 0.01 for cermet and −0.65 ± 0.01 for coated carbide) indicate surfaces dominated by valleys rather than peaks, which is consistent with the progressive flattening of asperities as the cutting edge loses sharpness. This suggests that peak removal is a common outcome for both tool materials under the tested cutting conditions. Furthermore, the kurtosis values below the Gaussian reference (Sku = 2.19 ± 0.02 for cermet and 2.17 ± 0.01 for coated carbide) reveal that the surfaces do not contain extreme height variations such as deep scratches or isolated sharp peaks. These results indicate that, despite the differences in tool wear, the machining process resulted in relatively uniform textures.

These additional roughness parameters help explain the functional behavior of the machined surfaces. The predominance of shallow valleys can improve lubricant retention in applications where tribological performance is relevant, while the absence of extreme peaks reduces the risk of localized stress concentrations during contact. In this context, the coated carbide tool, which generated lower R a,  R z , and R t  values, produced a surface that is not only smoother but also more favorable from a functional standpoint. Although the cermet tool showed significantly higher flank wear, its Ssk and Sku values remained similar to those of the coated carbide tool, indicating that the increased wear primarily affected the overall amplitude of the roughness rather than introducing severe topographical defects. This observation reinforces the conclusion that tool wear plays a decisive role in determining the magnitude of the roughness parameters, while the general shape of the height distribution remained comparable between tools.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, the cutting performance of single layer TiN coated cermet and multilayer TiN/Al 2 O 3 /TiCN coated carbide inserts was evaluated during the turning of HC-HSi cast steel. The results indicate that tool performance is strongly dependent on cutting conditions and tool material.

The cermet tool showed lower cutting-force components under less severe cutting conditions, whereas the coated carbide tool performed better at higher cutting speeds and feed rates, exhibiting lower cutting forces and improved surface quality. Feed rate and tool type significantly affected the R a  and R z  parameters, with better surface integrity achieved by the coated carbide tool as feed rate increased. Higher chip temperatures observed for the cermet tool are attributed to its lower thermal conductivity, which reduces heat dissipation during machining. Overall, the multilayer coated carbide tool proved to be more suitable for machining HC-HSi steel owing to its superior performance in terms of cutting forces, surface quality, and thermal behavior. The improved performance may be associated with its multilayer coating structure and the presence of oxide layers, which enhance thermal and mechanical stability.
